summary: A collection of Middle Eastern tales told inside a frame story. The ruler Schahriar has taken to marrying a wife each day and having her put to death. Scheherazade, the vizier's daughter, volunteers to marry him and keeps him from killing her by telling a story each night and leaving it unfinished. Within her telling come the Merchant and the Genius, the Fisherman, the Three Calenders, the Seven Voyages of Sindbad, Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp, and many more. This is Andrew Lang's selection for young readers, not the full set of nights.
context: No single canonical text of the Nights exists. Scholars trace its core to Indian and Persian tales put into Arabic perhaps in the early eighth century, with Arab stories and Harun al-Rashid tales added in Iraq by the ninth or tenth century, and more layers from Syria and Egypt from the thirteenth. The first English edition dates from about 1706 to 1721. Aladdin and Ali Baba were added by the French translator Antoine Galland and are not in the original Arabic versions. Andrew Lang (1844 to 1912), a Scottish writer, made this edition, and the site carries it.

timeline.label: Indian and Persian tales are probably put into Arabic around the early eighth century as Alf Layla.
In Iraq, Arab stories including Harun al-Rashid tales are added to the core.
A further layer of stories is added in Syria and Egypt from the thirteenth century.
The first English edition begins appearing, running to 1721.
Andrew Lang, compiler of this edition, is born.

ideas.title: Stories delay execution
ideas.note: Scheherazade tells tales to stay alive, a device with roots in earlier Indian frame stories.

ideas.title: A book with no fixed text
ideas.note: The Nights has no canonical order or number of tales, and editions differ.

ideas.title: Tales nested in tales
ideas.note: Some stories are framed within other tales while others are self-contained.

passages.why: Introduces Scheherazade and her sister Dinarzade.

passages.quote: Sindbad had adventures which perhaps came out of the Odyssey of Homer; in fact, all the East had contributed its wonders, and sent them to Europe in one parcel
passages.why: Lang's preface on where the tales came from.
